claim: Reviewed supervised learning approaches for ADAS driver-intent prediction using eye-tracking gaze data sampled at 5-second intervals.
detail: Examined how Artificial Neural Networks, Bayesian Networks, and Naive Bayes Classifiers balance maneuver prediction accuracy against false-alarm cognitive load.

claim: Compiled a thematic outline and annotated bibliography of nine peer-reviewed studies on cognitive load, working memory, and driving safety.
detail: Reviewed experimental research using lane change tests, eye tracking, closed-course driving tracks, and Apple CarPlay and Android Auto interfaces.

claim: Studied how Cognitive Load Theory, the modality effect, and automaticity govern dual-task visual and auditory distraction while driving.
detail: Examined working memory processes of updating, shifting, and inhibition alongside age-related visual perception factors in older drivers.

claim: Analyzed response times across four participants to evaluate whether illusion presentation order or fatigue influenced pattern recognition.
detail: Results supported the null hypothesis on sequence order, with three participants recognizing patterns in 5 to 8 seconds and one fatigued participant in 10 to 12 seconds.

claim: Analyzed screen-size and context-aware infotainment studies to formulate cognitive load reduction guidelines for in-car UI.
detail: Compared findings from a 48-participant Carrio 7-inch vs. 4.5-inch phone study and Volvo Intelligent News to recommend haptic, minimal-step HMI flows.

claim: Authored a research paper analyzing how in-car infotainment systems affect driver working memory, cognitive load, and road safety.
detail: Synthesized empirical studies on full-touch HMIs, context-aware infotainment, screen size, and gaze-based ADAS to propose interface safety guidelines.

claim: Analyzed classical HCI laws and cognitive models—including Fitts' Law, Hick-Hyman Law, GOMS, and mental models—for UI design.
detail: Evaluated predictive model limits against heuristic evaluation and cognitive walkthroughs across interface execution and evaluation gulfs.

claim: Explored contemporary HCI theories—embodied interaction, tangible manipulation, and in-the-wild research—and their accessibility implications.
detail: Connected theoretical frameworks to steering-wheel hand controls for drivers with disabilities and abstract artifacts in brain-computer interfaces.

claim: Researched how in-car infotainment systems impact driver working memory and cause distraction through cognitive overload.
detail: Reviewed in-vehicle platforms including Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, Carrio, and Volvo Intelligent News across task management and planning demands.

claim: Evaluated cognitive-load reduction strategies for in-car infotainment using simplified task flows, UI design, error prevention, and ADAS.
detail: Examined gaze detection methods—Artificial Neural Networks, Bayesian Networks, and Naive Bayes Classifiers—alongside hardware and software design.

claim: Studied modern HCI frameworks including distributed cognition, contextual design, situated action, ethnography, and grounded theory.
detail: Examined how external cognition, activity theory, and open, axial, and selective coding uncover workplace context and social coordination.

claim: Evaluated closed-circuit studies comparing full-touch in-vehicle HMIs against physical buttons across 50, 80, and 130 kmph speeds.
detail: Documented how full-touch controls increase saccades and pupil dilation, whereas physical controls leverage muscle memory to reduce visual distraction.

claim: Ran a controlled visual perception study with four participants testing Gestalt closure and optical illusions on a 1920x1080 display.
detail: Presented Hermann, Ehrenstein, and Coffer illusions in varied sequences at 250 nits in one-on-one sessions to test presentation-order effects.
